facts.claim: RFC 20 (1969) set out ASCII for network interchange: a 7-bit code, so 128 characters, numbered 0 to 127.
The Unicode Consortium’s page for Unicode 18.0, dated 16 September 2026: it adds 13,007 characters, for a total of 172,808.
Unicode’s glossary: the codespace is the range of integers from 0 to 10FFFF in hex, which is 1,114,112 code points.
RFC 3629: UTF-8 writes each character in 1 to 4 octets (bytes), and US-ASCII characters as one byte each, unchanged.
W3Techs, 30 October 2026: UTF-8 is used by 99.1% of all the websites whose character encoding they know.
The WHATWG Encoding Standard maps the labels “latin1” and “iso-8859-1” to windows-1252, so browsers read Latin-1 as Windows-1252.
ECMAScript: a string is a sequence of 16-bit code units, so a character past U+FFFF counts as two in its length.
Unicode’s UAX #29 defines grapheme clusters: what a reader takes as one character, such as emoji joined by zero-width joiners.
ECMA-402’s Intl.Segmenter splits a string into graphemes, words or sentences in the browser.
Unicode’s UAX #15: NFC composes, so e followed by a combining acute becomes the single code point é, and equivalent strings come out the same.
Unicode’s UTS #39 lists confusables: characters from different scripts that look alike, such as Latin a and Cyrillic а.
Radford et al. (2019) built GPT-2’s vocabulary over UTF-8 bytes, so any text can be turned into tokens.
